definition: How high or low a sound is; set by its frequency.
The number of vibrations per second, in hertz; heard as pitch.
The interval between a note and the note with twice its frequency; notes an octave apart share a letter name.
The smallest step on a piano, one twelfth of an octave in equal temperament (100 cents).
Two semitones.
A unit of pitch interval: 1200 per octave, 100 per equal-tempered semitone.
The colour of a sound that lets two instruments playing the same pitch sound different; set mainly by the mixture of partials.
The partials of a tone at whole-number multiples of its fundamental frequency: f, 2f, 3f, …
The lowest partial of a tone, which sets its pitch.
One of the frequencies a vibrating instrument sounds at once; for strings and winds, multiples of the fundamental.
The five lines and four spaces on which notes are written; higher position means higher pitch.
The sign at the start of a staff that fixes which line is which note: treble (G) clef, bass (F) clef, or a C clef.
A sharp, flat or natural written before a note, raising, lowering or restoring it for the rest of the bar.
Two names for the same key on a piano, such as F♯ and G♭.
The C near the middle of the piano, about 261.6 Hz; written on a ledger line between the treble and bass staves.
The steady pulse of music that you tap along to.
The speed of the beat, in beats per minute (BPM).
The grouping of beats into bars of strong and weak beats, shown by the time signature.
The two numbers at the start of a piece: beats per bar and the note value of one beat (or, in compound meter, how each beat divides).
A meter whose beats divide into three, such as 6/8 or 12/8.
A meter whose beats divide into two, such as 2/4, 3/4 or 4/4.
An accent where the meter does not expect one: on a weak beat or between beats.
Three equal notes in the time normally taken by two.
Two different pulses sounding at once, such as three against two.
Six beats regrouped from two groups of three into three groups of two, so two bars of 3/4 sound like one of 3/2.
Playing pairs of eighth notes long–short, roughly like the first and last of a triplet.
The distance between two pitches, named by number (third, fifth) and quality (major, minor, perfect, augmented, diminished).
An interval of seven semitones, frequency ratio about 3:2.
An interval of five semitones, ratio about 4:3.
An interval of four semitones, ratio about 5:4.
An interval of three semitones, ratio about 6:5.
An interval of six semitones, half an octave; the unstable interval at the heart of the dominant seventh chord.
Turning an interval upside down by moving one note an octave; the two intervals add up to an octave.
An interval wider than an octave, such as a ninth (octave plus a second).
An interval or chord that sounds stable and needs no resolution.
An interval or chord that sounds tense and, in tonal music, resolves to a consonance.
The harsh quality of two tones whose partials are close but not equal in frequency.
The seven-note scale with steps whole–whole–half–whole–whole–whole–half.
A note's position in its scale, numbered 1 to 7 (tonic, supertonic, mediant, subdominant, dominant, submediant, leading tone).
The first degree of a scale and the home note or chord of a key.
The fifth degree of a scale, or the chord built on it, which pulls strongly back to the tonic.
The fourth degree of a scale, or the chord built on it.
The seventh degree of a major scale, a semitone below the tonic and pulling up to it.
The tonal centre of a piece together with the scale it mainly uses.
The sharps or flats at the start of each line that apply to the whole piece.
The twelve keys arranged so each is a fifth from its neighbours; adjacent keys differ by one sharp or flat.
The minor scale with steps whole–half–whole–whole–half–whole–whole.
Natural minor with a raised seventh degree, giving a leading tone and an augmented second.
Minor with raised sixth and seventh degrees going up (and, classically, natural minor coming down).
A major and a minor key that share a key signature, such as C major and A minor.
A major and a minor key with the same tonic, such as C major and C minor.
A scale formed by starting the major scale's pattern on another degree: Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Locrian.
The mode on the second degree of the major scale: minor with a raised sixth.
The mode on the third degree: minor with a lowered second.
The mode on the fourth degree: major with a raised fourth.
The mode on the fifth degree: major with a lowered seventh.
The mode on the seventh degree: minor with lowered second and fifth.
A five-note scale; the major pentatonic leaves out the 4th and 7th of the major scale.
The minor pentatonic with an added flattened fifth (the blue note).
A six-note scale of whole steps only.
An eight-note scale alternating half and whole steps.
Three or more notes sounded together.
A three-note chord of a root, a third and a fifth: major, minor, diminished or augmented.
The note a chord is built on and named after.
A triad with a seventh above the root added.
A major triad with a minor seventh (G B D F in C); the chord that leads most strongly to the tonic.
A major triad with a major seventh (C E G B).
A diminished triad with a minor seventh (B D F A).
A chord of stacked minor thirds (B D F A♭); every note can act as a leading tone.
The label naming a chord by the scale degree of its root, upper case for major and lower case for minor.
A chord with a note other than its root in the bass.
Baroque shorthand naming chords by the intervals above the bass note.
How a chord's notes are arranged: their octaves, spacing and doubling.
A chord note above the seventh: the ninth, eleventh or thirteenth.
A chord with the third replaced by the fourth (sus4) or second (sus2).
A name such as Cmaj7 or G7♭9 that tells a player which chord to build.
A chord's role in a key: tonic (stable), predominant (moving away) or dominant (pulling home).
A series of chords.
The rate at which the chords change.
The chords that end a phrase: authentic, half, plagal or deceptive.
A phrase ending V–I; perfect when both chords are in root position and the tonic is on top.
A phrase ending on V, sounding open.
IV–I, the 'Amen' ending.
V–vi: the expected tonic replaced by its substitute.
The way each note of one chord moves to the next, so every part makes a good line.
Two voices a perfect fifth (or octave) apart moving in the same direction to another; avoided in classical voice leading.
A melody note outside the chord, such as a passing tone, neighbour tone or suspension.
A note held over a change of chord, becoming a dissonance that resolves down by step.
An accented dissonance approached by leap and resolved by step.
A note held, usually in the bass, while the harmony changes above it.
The dominant of a chord other than the tonic, used to make that chord sound briefly like a tonic.
Making a chord sound briefly like a tonic, usually with its secondary dominant, without changing key.
A change of key confirmed by a cadence in the new key.
A chord belonging to both the old and the new key, used to modulate smoothly.
Using chords from the parallel key, such as iv or ♭VI in a major key.
A major tonic chord at the end of a piece in a minor key.
A major chord on the lowered second degree, usually in first inversion, leading to the dominant.
A predominant chord whose augmented sixth (♭6̂ and ♯4̂) expands outward to the octave on the dominant.
The combination of independent melodic lines.
The fixed melody against which counterpoint is written.
Fux's five-step method of learning counterpoint, from note-against-note to free.
Two voices moving in opposite directions.
Strict imitation: a melody followed exactly by another voice entering later.
A contrapuntal piece in which a subject enters in every voice in turn and is then developed.
The smallest recognisable musical idea.
A complete musical thought ending in a cadence.
Two phrases paired as question (ending weakly) and answer (ending strongly).
An eight-bar theme: a two-bar idea, its repetition, and a four-bar continuation to a cadence.
A piece in two sections, AB, each usually repeated.
A piece in three sections, ABA.
A form in which a refrain returns between contrasting episodes (ABACA).
The form of most Classical first movements: exposition, development and recapitulation.
The twelve-bar chord pattern I–I–I–I, IV–IV–I–I, V–IV–I–V.
The 32-bar song form of four eight-bar sections, the third (B) being the bridge.
The basic jazz progression: supertonic seventh, dominant seventh, tonic.
The thirds and sevenths of chords, which define their quality and move by step through a progression.
Matching each chord with a scale containing its chord tones and available tensions.
Replacing a dominant seventh chord with the one a tritone away, which shares its tritone.
Replacing a tune's chords with others that keep its melody and function.
Tuning intervals to small whole-number ratios such as 3/2 and 5/4.
The small interval 81/80 (about 21.5 cents) between four pure fifths and a pure major third plus two octaves.
The gap of about 23.5 cents by which twelve pure fifths overshoot seven octaves.
A tuning built entirely from pure 3:2 fifths.
The badly out-of-tune fifth left over in Pythagorean or meantone tuning.
A tuning that adjusts some pure intervals so the others fit.
Dividing the octave into twelve equal semitones, each a ratio of 2^(1/12).
A tuning with fifths narrowed so that major thirds are pure.
An unequal tuning in which every key is usable but each has its own colour.
All pitches with the same name in every octave, numbered 0 (C) to 11 (B).
An interval and its inversion counted as one, numbered 0 to 6.
All the pitch-class sets related by transposition or inversion, named by Forte numbers and prime forms.
A list of how many intervals of each class a set contains.
An ordering of all twelve pitch classes used as the basis of a twelve-tone piece.
A row or melody played backwards.
